extracted.intended_audience: readers of the Notices of the AMS: mathematicians, computational mathematicians, and users of computer algebra systems (Derive, Maple, Mathematica, Reduce); also policy-interested mathematical scientists
extracted.subtask_description: A set of computer-algebra-system programming problems (Koch snowflake, Feigenbaum constant, combinatorial triples, prime listing, polynomial GCD over GF(27)) plus a policy column on setting science priorities. The page supplies problem specifications, expected outputs/values, and language-specific example implementations and commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Koch snowflake program specification
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a program to draw the Koch snowflake. Start with an equilateral triangle. At each stage go to the next by adding to each side an equilateral triangle pointing outwards of side 1/3 the size of the current edges, centered on the edge. Clearly you'll need to end the iteration after finitely many steps; that should be a parameter in the program.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implementation notes and examples provided for Derive (recursive definition using IF and EDGE/STAR), Maple (procedure Koch with helper Kpoint, plotting with AspectRatio and PLOT, example al6 := Koch(6)), and Mathematica (KochSnowflake[n] using FixedPoint and a doline helper). Reduce has no graphics. Guidance implies: accept an iteration-depth parameter, produce a drawing (EPS/BMP/WMF support noted for Mathematica), and recursive/iterative approaches are acceptable. The Derive example shows how to structure recursive EDGE and STAR definitions; Maple and Mathematica examples show array/curve or graphics-based constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feigenbaum number program specification
rubrics_metrics.description: Write a program to find the Feigenbaum number. Consider f(x)=a x (1-x). Define a(n) to be the smallest value of a for which f as a map of [0,1] to [0,1] has a cycle of order 2^n. Let a(∞) be their limit. The Feigenbaum number is lim {a(∞)-a(n)}/{a(∞)-a(n+1)}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derive: a sixteen-line program using IF, ITERATE, VECTOR was provided; Maple: roughly 50 lines; Mathematica: 27 lines with vendor example producing values (ginf == 3.569945671870944901842004, Feigenbaum constant == 4.669201609103). Reduce: elaborate multi-line program. Guidance implies: compute a(n) sequence robustly, approximate its limit, and compute the quoted ratio; numerical precision and iteration depth matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generate triples of integers with a bound condition (Problem 18)
rubrics_metrics.description: Write a program to generate a list of all triples of positive integers less than n with the property that the difference between the largest and smallest is not greater than 1/2 the middle one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple language examples: Derive one-line VECTOR expression; Maple: nested loops with condition 2*(k-i) <= j accumulating t[c]:=[i,j,k]; Mathematica: use Needs["DiscreteMath`Combinatorica`"] and Select[KSubsets[Range[n-1],3],((#[[3]]-#[[1]]) <= #[[2]]/2)&], then Join/Permutations/Map to get permutations and triples of identical elements. Reduce: nested loops with conditional ranges. Guidance implies: ensure correct inequality, consider whether permutations should be included (Mathematica example uses Permutations and also includes triples like {i,i,i}), and implement efficient iteration/selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: List primes in a given interval (Problem 19)
rubrics_metrics.description: Write a program to generate a list of primes between 100,000 and 101,000.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derive example uses PRIME_COUNT and PRIME..LIST defined via NEXT-PRIME and ITERATES; Maple example uses nextprime loop to collect primes; Mathematica uses Prime and PrimePi-based indexing (PrimesBetween[100000,101000]); Reduce uses ifprimep test in a join. The page notes there are 81 primes in the list. Guidance: language-specific prime-next or prime-count utilities are appropriate; handling endpoints and counting is part of the spec.

rubrics_metrics.name: GCD of polynomials over GF(27) (Problem 20)
rubrics_metrics.description: Write a program to find the GCD of two polynomials over the field of order 27.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maple example: implement Euclidean Algorithm and make the Gcd monic (GcdUniGFq := proc(a,b,x,p) ... while d <> a do r := Rem(c,d,x) mod p; c := d; d := r; Expand(cllcoeff(c,x)) mod p # Make the Gcd monic end:). Reduce: no general code for finite fields but has modulo arithmetic; one must set up the finite field (the field of 27 elements is gotten by adjoining an element of order 3 to Z3). Mathematica: a 50-line program provided. Guidance: correctly implement arithmetic in GF(3^3), ensure Euclidean algorithm uses field reduction at each step, and normalize the GCD to be monic; multivariate support noted in Maple sample.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize science funding only after well-defined goals are set
rubrics_metrics.description: Well-defined goals have to be established before priorities can be invested with meaning; witnesses at hearings emphasized that a more rational process for determining science budgets is desirable and that well-defined goals are a prerequisite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The OTA report and HSST task force stress that without explicit goals priority-setting is not meaningful. Practical implication: agencies and disciplines should state concrete goals before attempting to rank programs or request targeted funds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary criterion for funding basic research: scientific excellence
rubrics_metrics.description: For basic research, where level-of-effort (as opposed to goal-driven) programs predominate, the primary criterion for funding decisions is scientific excellence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies (e.g., NSF) still need specific justifications for budget increases even in basic research, but peer-assessed scientific excellence is presented as the core funding determinant for basic research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Involve the scientific community in assessing relative merits
rubrics_metrics.description: Because Congress is not well equipped to determine the scientific merit of R&D proposals, it relies on advice from the science community; several witnesses emphasized the importance of involving the scientific community in assessing relative merits of federal science programs, possibly via an iterative process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical measures include task forces, hearings, discipline-led bottom-up priority-setting exercises, and iterative consensus-building processes. The page cites disciplinary exercises (astronomy, ecology) as examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconcile top-down (federal) and bottom-up (discipline) priorities
rubrics_metrics.description: Top-down priorities imposed by entities like FCCSET need to be reconciled with bottom-up priorities coming from the scientific community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies and coordinating bodies must find mechanisms to align cross-agency directives with discipline-driven goals; the page highlights the need for coordination and the political reality of competing national goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require specific justifications and coordination when requesting budget increases
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must provide specific justifications for budget increases (even in basic research) and coordinate programs with other entities (states, other federal agencies, colleges and universities) to be responsible stewards of public funds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: NSF and NIH strategic planning that frame budgets in terms of national goals rather than raw counts of grants; justification should connect proposed spending to measurable national objectives and to inter-agency coordination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure progress toward stated goals
rubrics_metrics.description: A priority-setting exercise should include measures of progress toward goals; the HSST task force will likely focus on how to measure progress toward those goals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical implication: define metrics and monitoring processes as part of strategic planning so that prioritization can be evaluated against outcomes over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use consensus-building and advocacy to increase political traction for discipline priorities
rubrics_metrics.description: Discipline-level statements built by iterative consensus processes have political appeal and may fare well in the political process, but acceptance by agencies and Congress often depends on advocacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The astronomy example (priority ranking of facilities through iterative consensus) and ecology's 'sustainable biosphere initiative' are cited; practical guidance is to combine clear scientific goals with advocacy to gain traction in budget decisions.
